tp: For 120/80 mm Hg the pulse pressure is 40 mm Hg. It should be at least 25 percent of the systolic pressure.

ww.Mean arterial pressure: MAP is the average driving pressure, estimated as diastolic plus one-third of the pulse pressure.
ww.Hydrostatic pressure: Hydrostatic pressure is the general force a fluid exerts on its container; blood pressure is one form.

evidence: As shown in Figure 20.10, the difference between the systolic pressure and the diastolic pressure is the pulse pressure.

bw: Diastolic plus one-third of pulse pressure
tp: Normal MAP is 70–110 mm Hg. Below 60 mm Hg for an extended time, tissues become ischemic.

ww.Pulse pressure: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic.
ww.Systolic pressure: Systolic pressure is the peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction.

evidence: Although complicated to measure directly and complicated to calculate, MAP can be approximated by adding the diastolic pressure to one-third of the pulse pressure or systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure:

bw: MAP below 60 mm Hg for a long time
tp: Hypoxia, inadequate oxygenation of tissues, commonly accompanies ischemia. Neurons are especially sensitive to it.

ww.Hypoxemia: Hypoxemia is low oxygen in arterial blood, not insufficient flow.

evidence: If the value falls below 60 mm Hg for an extended time, blood pressure will not be high enough to ensure circulation to and through the tissues, which results in ischemia, or insufficient blood flow.

bw: Sounds heard while measuring blood pressure
tp: There are five recognized Korotkoff sounds but only two are normally recorded: the first (systolic) and the last (diastolic).

ww.Heart murmurs: Murmurs are abnormal heart sounds from turbulent flow in the heart.
ww.S1 and S2: S1 and S2 are heart sounds from valve closure.

evidence: Turbulent blood flow through the vessels can be heard as a soft ticking while measuring blood pressure; these sounds are known as Korotkoff sounds.

bw: First Korotkoff sound heard as the cuff deflates
tp: The last sound heard marks the diastolic pressure.

ww.Diastolic pressure: Diastolic pressure is the point where the last sound is heard.
ww.Mean arterial pressure: MAP is calculated, not read from a Korotkoff sound.

evidence: As shown in Figure 20.12, the first sound heard through the stethoscope—the first Korotkoff sound—indicates systolic pressure.

bw: Last Korotkoff sound heard as the cuff deflates
tp: After the last sound, blood flows freely through the brachial artery and all sounds disappear.

ww.Systolic pressure: Systolic pressure is read at the first sound.
ww.Pulse pressure: Pulse pressure is a difference calculated from two readings.

evidence: The point at which the last sound is heard is recorded as the patient’s diastolic pressure.

tp: Other causes of a low pulse pressure are aortic valve stenosis and significant blood loss after trauma.

ww.Strenuous exercise: Exercise temporarily widens the pulse pressure as stroke volume rises.
ww.Hypervolemia: Excess volume is not listed as a cause of a narrow pulse pressure.

evidence: This may occur, for example, in patients with a low stroke volume, which may be seen in congestive heart failure, stenosis of the aortic valve, or significant blood loss following trauma.

bw: Wide pulse pressure in a healthy person
tp: Resting pulse pressure of 30–40 mm Hg can reach 100 mm Hg temporarily. A persistently high value warrants treatment.

ww.During sleep: Nothing in the source links sleep to a wide pulse pressure.
ww.After blood loss: Blood loss lowers stroke volume and can narrow the pulse pressure.

evidence: In contrast, a high or wide pulse pressure is common in healthy people following strenuous exercise, when their resting pulse pressure of 30–40 mm Hg may increase temporarily to 100 mm Hg as stroke volume increases.

bw: Ability of a compartment to expand with more content
tp: Stiff arteries have reduced compliance, so resistance, turbulence and pressure rise and flow falls.

ww.Viscosity: Viscosity is the thickness of a fluid.
ww.Vascular resistance: Resistance is what impedes flow; low compliance raises it.

evidence: Compliance is the ability of any compartment to expand to accommodate increased content.

tp: Veins hold about 64 percent of the blood volume.

ww.Arteries: Arteries are less compliant than veins.
ww.Arterioles: Arterioles are resistance vessels, not the compliant reservoir.

evidence: Veins are more compliant than arteries and can expand to hold more blood.

bw: Artery constricts to half its radius
tp: Resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power. Doubling the radius cuts resistance to 1/16.

ww.Resistance doubles: Radius to the fourth power means a 16-fold change, not 2.

evidence: This means, for example, that if an artery or arteriole constricts to one-half of its original radius, the resistance to flow will increase 16 times.

bw: Most precipitous drop in blood pressure
tp: This is why arteriolar vasoconstriction and vasodilation regulate blood pressure more than changes in other vessels.

ww.Capillaries: Capillaries are smaller individually but so numerous that their total area is huge and resistance is lower overall.
ww.Venules: Venules sit after the capillaries, where pressure is already low.

evidence: However, the site of the most precipitous drop, and the site of greatest resistance, is the arterioles.

bw: Largest total cross-sectional area in the body
tp: One capillary is smaller than an arteriole, but there are vastly more capillaries than other vessels.

ww.Arterioles: Arterioles are far fewer than capillaries, so their total area is smaller.
ww.Veins: Veins are larger individually but much fewer in number than capillaries.

evidence: Notice in parts (a) and (b) that the total cross-sectional area of the body’s capillary beds is far greater than any other type of vessel.

tp: Velocity then rises again as blood returns to the heart through the veins.

ww.Arteries: Flow is fastest in the arteries.
ww.Veins: Velocity rises again in the veins.

evidence: Part (d) shows that the velocity (speed) of blood flow decreases dramatically as the blood moves from arteries to arterioles to capillaries.

tp: Patients may be asymptomatic until 10–20 percent of blood volume is lost. Treatment is IV fluid replacement.

ww.Hypoxemia: Hypoxemia is low arterial oxygen, not low volume.

evidence: Low blood volume, called hypovolemia, may be caused by bleeding, dehydration, vomiting, severe burns, or some medications used to treat hypertension.

tp: It results from retention of water and sodium; treatment means reversing the cause.

ww.Ischemia: Ischemia is insufficient blood flow to a tissue, not excess volume.

evidence: Hypervolemia, excessive fluid volume, may be caused by retention of water and sodium, as seen in patients with heart failure, liver cirrhosis, some forms of kidney disease, hyperaldosteronism, and some glucocorticoid steroid treatments.

tp: Think of sipping a milkshake versus milk through the same straw.

ww.Resistance and flow both up: Viscosity is directly proportional to resistance and inversely proportional to flow.

evidence: The viscosity of blood is directly proportional to resistance and inversely proportional to flow; therefore, any condition that causes viscosity to increase will also increase resistance and decrease flow.

bw: Contractile state of vascular smooth muscle
tp: Diameter, through the radius term, changes resistance and flow dramatically and quickly, unlike vessel length or viscosity.

ww.Compliance: Compliance is the ability to expand under added volume.
ww.Viscosity: Viscosity is the thickness of the blood and changes slowly.

evidence: The vascular tone of the vessel is the contractile state of the smooth muscle and the primary determinant of diameter, and thus of resistance and flow.

bw: Returns blood to the heart against gravity
tp: Valves above the contracting muscle open while valves below close, so blood moves upward.

ww.Respiratory pump: The respiratory pump uses pressure changes in the thorax during breathing.
ww.Atrial kick: The atrial kick is atrial contraction adding to ventricular filling.

evidence: This mechanism, known as the skeletal muscle pump (Figure 20.15), helps the lower-pressure veins counteract the force of gravity, increasing pressure to move blood back to the heart.

tp: During inhalation, thoracic vein pressure falls below abdominal vein pressure, so blood flows up into the thorax.

ww.Skeletal muscle pump: The skeletal muscle pump works by muscle contraction around the veins of the limbs.
ww.Venoconstriction: Venoconstriction is narrowing of vein walls by smooth muscle, not a breathing mechanism.

evidence: The respiratory pump aids blood flow through the veins of the thorax and abdomen.

bw: Effect on blood return to the heart
tp: Unlike arteries, rounder constricted veins offer less resistance, so higher venous pressure increases flow and preload.

ww.Decreases venous return: Constricting veins increases flow toward the low-pressure atria.
ww.Decreases preload: Venoconstriction increases preload, the stretch of cardiac muscle.

evidence: Thus, venoconstriction increases the return of blood to the heart.

bw: Buildup of cholesterol, calcium and debris in the artery wall
tp: Plaque can rupture and clot, causing heart attack or stroke, or break off as an embolus.

ww.Aneurysm: An aneurysm is a bulging weakened wall, not plaque buildup.
ww.Vasospasm: Vasospasm is temporary vessel constriction, not plaque.

evidence: The term for this condition, atherosclerosis (athero- = “porridge”) describes the mealy deposits (Figure 20.14).

bw: Balloon-tipped catheter widens a narrowed vessel
tp: A stent, a small mesh tube, is often inserted to prevent the vessel from collapsing again.

ww.Endarterectomy: Endarterectomy surgically removes plaque from the vessel wall.
ww.Coronary bypass: A bypass creates a path around the blocked area using another vessel.

evidence: In angioplasty, a catheter is inserted into the vessel at the point of narrowing, and a second catheter with a balloon-like tip is inflated to widen the opening.

bw: Plaque surgically removed from vessel walls
Often done on the carotid arteries
tp: The carotid arteries are a prime source of oxygenated blood for the brain.

ww.Angioplasty: Angioplasty widens the vessel with a balloon catheter rather than removing plaque.
ww.Coronary bypass: A coronary bypass routes blood around a blocked coronary artery.

evidence: In an endarterectomy, plaque is surgically removed from the walls of a vessel.
